lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Landforms and the Plants and Animals That Live in Them

pages.body:
Ghana is a country of great variety. Drive north from Accra and the dense green forest gradually gives way to open grassland and thorny trees. Travel east and you climb into cooler, mist-covered hills. Follow the Volta River and you descend into lush valleys where crocodiles bask on muddy banks.

- What kinds of plants and animals do you expect to find in the area where you live?
- Why do you think different plants and animals live in different places?
- Have you ever visited a very different part of Ghana — the north, a river valley or a forested hill? What did you notice about the plants and animals there?

> **DEFINITION** **Landform:** a natural physical feature of the Earth's surface, such as a mountain, plain, valley or plateau. **Habitat:** the specific environment in which an organism lives and finds the food, water and shelter it needs. **Adaptation:** a feature of an organism's body or behaviour that makes it suited to surviving in its particular habitat.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: The Plateau

pages.title: The Plateau
pages.body:
A plateau is a high, flat area of land raised significantly above the surrounding countryside. In Ghana, the Kwahu Plateau in the Eastern Region is the most well-known, rising to about 760 metres above sea level. The Gambaga Escarpment in the Northern Region is another important plateau landform.

Plateaus are generally cooler than the surrounding lowlands because of their altitude. They often receive more rainfall than the plains below, but the wind can be strong. Soils on plateaus are often thinner and more exposed than in valleys.

The plants you find on Ghanaian plateaus are adapted to these cooler, windier conditions. Grasses are common, along with low shrubs and scattered small trees that can tolerate drier conditions on exposed slopes. Some areas of the Kwahu Plateau still support patches of moist forest in sheltered areas.

Animals on plateaus tend to be swift-moving or able to use the elevation to their advantage. Eagles and hawks circle the Kwahu heights, using rising air currents to soar while hunting. Antelopes and small mammals graze on the grasses. Reptiles such as lizards are common on rocky outcrops, using the sun-warmed stones to regulate their body temperature.

> **Did you know?** The Kwahu Plateau is famous in Ghana not just for its scenery but for Easter celebrations, when thousands of people travel there to enjoy the cool air, paragliding and the breathtaking views over the valleys below.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: The Plain

pages.title: The Plain
pages.body:
A plain is a large area of flat or gently rolling land at a low altitude. Ghana's northern savanna plain is the country's largest landform, stretching across the Northern, Upper East and Upper West Regions. The Accra Plains along the south-eastern coast and the Volta Basin are other important plains.

Plains in northern Ghana experience a long dry season and a shorter rainy season. Temperatures are high and rainfall is lower than in the forest south. This gives rise to the classic savanna landscape: a mixture of grasses and scattered trees capable of tolerating drought.

The trees most associated with Ghanaian plains are the baobab, whose enormous trunk stores water, and various acacia species with their characteristic flat, umbrella-shaped canopies. Grasses grow tall and green during the rains and dry to golden-brown in the dry season. Shea trees are economically important on the plains, producing shea nuts for oil and butter.

Animal life on the plains is rich and varied. Cattle, goats and sheep are kept by pastoral farmers and are well suited to walking long distances in search of pasture and water. Wild animals include various species of antelope, foxes, guinea fowl, francolins, snakes and a huge diversity of insects. Birds of prey such as kestrels hunt for rodents and grasshoppers in the open grassland. Termites build large mounds that serve as homes for many other animals.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: The Mountain and Hills

pages.title: The Mountain and Hills
pages.body:
Ghana does not have very high mountains, but it has several ranges of forested hills that create a significantly different environment from the lowlands. The Atewa Range in the Eastern Region, the Akwapim-Togo Range running north-east from Accra, and the hills around the Volta gorge are Ghana's most important hilly landforms.

These hill ranges receive high rainfall and are significantly cooler than the surrounding lowlands. The combination of moisture and temperature creates conditions for dense rainforest to grow, particularly in sheltered valleys on the hillsides. The Atewa Range is one of Ghana's most biodiverse forest reserves, home to species found nowhere else on Earth.

The forest plants on Ghana's hill ranges are tall, with closed canopies that prevent most sunlight from reaching the forest floor. Trees such as mahogany, odum and African teak grow here. Under the canopy, ferns, mosses and epiphytic plants (those that grow on other plants without harming them) thrive in the humid conditions. Orchids cling to branches and tree trunks, getting their moisture from the humid air.

Animal life in the hill forests is rich but harder to see than on the open plains. Monkeys — including mona monkeys and olive colobus monkeys — live in the tree canopy. Forest elephants pass through Atewa. The diversity of birds in these hill forests is exceptional, with hornbills, sunbirds, turacos and many endemic species. Chameleons cling to branches, their colour-changing skin making them almost invisible. Butterflies of extraordinary variety flutter through forest glades, and many unusual frogs live in the damp leaf litter.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: The Valley

pages.title: The Valley
pages.body:
A valley is a low-lying area of land between hills or mountains, typically formed by a river over thousands or millions of years. Ghana's most important valleys are those of the Volta River and its tributaries — the Black Volta, White Volta, Oti and Afram Rivers. The Pra, Ankobra and Tano river valleys in the southern forest zone are also significant.

River valleys in Ghana are among the most productive and biologically rich environments in the country. The soil in river valleys is often deep, fertile and moist, deposited by floods over centuries. Temperatures are moderate and the presence of permanent water supports a much wider variety of life than the dry plains nearby.

Plants in river valleys include species that can tolerate flooding, heavy soils and high moisture. Gallery forest — dense tree growth along river banks — provides shade and stabilises the river banks. Water plants such as reeds, bulrushes and water hyacinth grow at the water's edge. The roots of riverside trees reach deep into the bank to access water while anchoring against erosion.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Landforms and the Plants and Animals That Live in Them (part 6)

pages.body:
Valleys are home to Ghana's most spectacular large animals. Hippopotamuses live in and around the Volta River and its tributaries, spending their days in the water and grazing on river bank vegetation at night. Nile crocodiles are found along most of Ghana's large rivers. Herons, kingfishers and fish eagles hunt along the water's edge. Fish — including tilapia, catfish and the enormous Nile perch — fill the rivers. Frogs, monitor lizards and freshwater turtles are common. The rich vegetation of valley forests supports populations of forest animals including monkeys, bushbuck and forest duikers.

> **Lesson 1 Assessment**

questions.q: Which of the following correctly defines a plateau?
o: A low-lying area of land between hills, usually formed by a river
A large, flat-topped area of land raised significantly above the surrounding countryside
A broad, flat area of land at low altitude covering a large area
A steep-sided hill with a narrow top

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a plateau landform in Ghana?
o: The Volta River basin
The Accra Plains
The Kwahu Plateau
The Atewa forest valley

questions.q: Why does the baobab tree store water in its trunk?
o: To attract animals that come to drink from it
Because it lives in a valley where water is always available
To survive the long dry season on the plains, where water is scarce for months
Because it cannot absorb water through its roots

questions.q: Which of the following animals would you most likely find living in a river valley in Ghana?
o: Guinea fowl and antelopes
Crocodiles, hippopotamuses and herons
Eagles soaring on wind currents
Desert-adapted rodents

questions.q: Which type of plant is described as growing on other plants without harming them?
o: Parasitic plant
Epiphyte
Water plant
Carnivorous plant

questions.q: Why is animal life in Ghana's hill forests harder to observe than on the open plains?
o: There are fewer animals in the forest than on the plains
Forest animals are smaller than savanna animals
The dense tree canopy conceals animals and they can hide among trees and leaves
Forest animals are nocturnal and never come out during the day

questions.q: What is gallery forest?
o: A forest planted around an art gallery
Dense tree growth along the banks of a river in an otherwise open landscape
A cleared area in the forest used for exhibitions
A type of mountain forest found only in Ghana

questions.q: The Atewa Range in Ghana is significant because:
o: It is the highest mountain in Ghana, reaching over 3,000 metres
It is one of Ghana's most biodiverse forest reserves, home to species found nowhere else
It is the site of Ghana's largest hydroelectric dam
It is an example of a flat plain in the Eastern Region

questions.q: Which of the following best explains why the valleys of Ghana's rivers support such a wide variety of life?
o: Valleys receive less rainfall than other landforms, forcing animals to cluster together
Valley soils are deep, fertile and moist; permanent water is available and temperatures are moderate
Valleys are warmer and drier than plateaus, making them suitable for desert species
Valleys have no trees and open space allows animals to spread out

questions.q: Which bird is specifically associated with hunting fish along Ghana's river valleys?
o: Guinea fowl
Hornbill
Fish eagle
Weaver bird

questions.q: Eagles and hawks are commonly found on the Kwahu Plateau because:
o: They prefer cold weather and cannot survive in warm valleys
They use the rising warm air currents from the plateau to soar while scanning for prey below
They are unable to fly at lower altitudes
The plateau has more water than the valleys

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical plant of Ghana's northern savanna plains?
o: Baobab tree
Acacia tree
Shea tree
Mangrove tree

questions.q: Define a landform and name the four main types of landform studied in this lesson.
Describe the Kwahu Plateau. Where is it found, how high is it, and what type of climate does it have?
Name three plants found on Ghana's savanna plains and briefly describe what each one looks like.
Explain what makes the Atewa Range special for biodiversity in Ghana.
Describe the typical animals found in a river valley in Ghana. Name at least four species.
Explain what an epiphyte is and give one example found in Ghana's hill forests.
Describe how the climate of Ghana's northern plains differs from that of the hill forests in the Eastern Region.
What is gallery forest and why is it important for the organisms living in a valley?
Explain why the soil in river valleys is typically more fertile than the soil on plateaus.
Name two animals found on Ghana's savanna plains and describe one feature of each that helps it survive there.
Explain why different landforms in Ghana support different types of plants and animals.

A wildlife photographer visits Ghana and wants to photograph the greatest possible variety of organisms. She has time to visit only two of the four landforms. Which two would you recommend she visit, and why? Support your answer with specific organisms she would find at each location.

A farmer on the northern plains wants to plant trees on his farm to provide shade and improve the soil. Based on what you know about the plants naturally adapted to the plain, suggest two suitable tree species and explain why each would be well suited to that landform.

Nature observation walk: Walk around your school compound or a nearby area for 20 minutes. List every plant and animal you observe, noting where exactly each one was found (e.g. on the ground, in a tree, at the edge of water). Classify your school grounds as resembling which landform and explain your classification.

Landform research: Research one of the four landforms in more detail, focusing on Ghana. Find out: its location in Ghana, its climate, three plants and three animals found there, and one interesting fact about this landform's ecology. Write a one-page report.

Class album — Landforms of Ghana: Each student draws or collects images of one plant and one animal from each of the four landforms. Compile these into a class album with a page for each landform, labelled with the organism's name, landform, and one survival adaptation. Display the album in the classroom.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: How Plants and Animals Survive in Their Landforms

pages.body:
A cactus placed in a river valley would quickly die from too much water around its roots. A water lily placed on a dry plateau would wither within hours. A valley crocodile would find it impossible to survive on a windswept plateau. Every organism is designed — through millions of years of evolution — to fit its particular environment perfectly.

- Think of one plant in your community. What feature of that plant allows it to survive there — its thick stem, its deep roots, its waxy leaves?
- Think of one animal. What body feature or behaviour helps it survive — its camouflage, its ability to run fast, its thick skin?

> **DEFINITION** **Adaptation:** a feature of an organism's body, physiology or behaviour that improves its ability to survive and reproduce in its specific habitat. **Structural adaptation:** a physical feature of an organism's body that helps it survive, such as thick bark, deep roots or waterproof skin. **Behavioural adaptation:** an action or pattern of behaviour that helps an organism survive, such as migrating, hibernating or hunting at night.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Plant survival characteristics on the plateau

pages.title: Plant survival characteristics on the plateau
pages.body:
Plateau plants face strong winds, cooler temperatures, thinner soils and periodic water stress when rain is scarce. Grasses on the plateau have narrow, tough leaves that lose little water through evaporation and flex in the wind rather than snapping. Their root systems are extensive and fibrous, spreading widely through shallow soil to capture every drop of rain.

Shrubs that grow on the plateau have small, waxy leaves with a thick outer cuticle that reduces water loss. Some plateau plants grow low to the ground to stay out of the strongest winds. Trees on exposed parts of the plateau tend to have deep tap roots that reach down through the rocky soil to access groundwater far below the surface.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Plant survival characteristics on the plain

pages.title: Plant survival characteristics on the plain
pages.body: Savanna plants face the most extreme challenge: surviving a dry season that can last six months or more, when temperatures are high and there is almost no rain. The baobab is the master of this environment. Its enormous trunk is a water storage organ, holding thousands of litres of water during the rains for use during the dry season. Its bark is thick and fire-resistant, protecting the tree from the bush fires that sweep across the savanna during the dry season.

Acacia trees have thorns to deter animals from eating their leaves, and very small leaflets that reduce water loss. Their roots are extensive both deep and wide. Many savanna grasses die back entirely above the ground during the dry season, surviving as root systems that burst into growth as soon as the first rains arrive. This fire-dependent lifestyle means grasses actually need occasional burning to clear away dead material and release nutrients.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Plant survival characteristics on the mountain and hills

pages.title: Plant survival characteristics on the mountain and hills
pages.body: Mountain forest plants in Ghana have the opposite challenge from savanna plants — they must thrive in high humidity, reduced light and occasional strong winds. Tall forest trees such as mahogany compete intensely for light by growing straight and tall, producing leaves only near the top where sunlight reaches. Their buttress roots — large flange-like extensions at the base of the trunk — spread widely to anchor the tree in shallow forest soils and to absorb nutrients from the thin leaf litter layer.

On the forest floor, shade-adapted plants such as ferns and mosses can photosynthesise in very low light conditions using large, thin, dark-green leaves that capture every available photon. Epiphytes like orchids and bromeliads have specialised roots that absorb moisture from humid air rather than from soil. These plants have no soil root system at all, yet thrive on tree branches many metres above the ground.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Plant survival characteristics in the valley

pages.title: Plant survival characteristics in the valley
pages.body: Valley plants must cope with waterlogged soils, periodic flooding and the weight and force of moving water. Riverside trees like the red mangrove (found in coastal valleys and estuaries) have prop roots — a tangle of arching roots that emerge from the trunk and lower branches, spreading out into the mud to provide stability in unstable, waterlogged ground. These roots also help the tree access oxygen in oxygen-poor muddy soils.

Reed beds and bulrushes grow in the shallower edges of rivers and lakes. Their hollow, air-filled stems carry oxygen down to the roots, which would otherwise suffocate in waterlogged mud. Water hyacinth, a floating plant, has air-filled leaf stalks that act like life jackets, keeping the plant buoyant. Many valley plants have flexible stems that bend with water currents rather than snapping.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Animal survival characteristics on the plateau

pages.title: Animal survival characteristics on the plateau
pages.body: Animals on the plateau use the elevation to their advantage for scanning the landscape. Eagles have exceptional eyesight — they can spot a small rodent from hundreds of metres in the air. Their broad wings are adapted to use thermals (rising columns of warm air) for effortless soaring above the plateau. Plateau antelopes are fast runners, using their long legs and split hooves to sprint across rocky ground. Their colouring is typically pale brown, blending with the dry grassland to reduce their visibility to predators.

pages.title: Animal survival characteristics on the plain
pages.body:
The savanna plain is a land of extremes, and its animals are adapted accordingly. Many savanna animals can go for long periods without water, or travel great distances to find it. Cattle and other livestock on the northern plains are often of breeds such as the West African Dwarf cattle, which are naturally tolerant of high temperatures and the trypanosome parasite (sleeping sickness) carried by tsetse flies.

Grasshoppers and other insects have camouflage colouring that exactly matches the dry grass around them, making them nearly invisible to predators. Their hard exoskeletons resist desiccation (drying out). Snakes on the plains are often heat-resistant and capable of slowing their metabolism during the hottest part of the day, becoming active in the cooler morning and evening hours.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Animal survival characteristics on the mountain and hills

pages.title: Animal survival characteristics on the mountain and hills
pages.body: Animals in Ghana's hill forests have evolved to live in a three-dimensional world of branches, vines and tree trunks. Monkeys such as the mona monkey and olive colobus have long limbs and a powerful grip — their hands and feet can grasp branches from multiple angles, allowing them to move rapidly through the canopy. Their prehensile tails in some species act as a fifth limb.

Chameleons are among the most specialised forest animals. Their laterally compressed bodies allow them to move along thin branches without falling. Their tong-like feet grip branches from either side. Their independently moving eyes allow them to look in two directions at once, giving almost all-round vision without turning their head. Their colour-changing skin provides camouflage against bark and leaves. Forest birds tend to have rounded wings for manoeuvring through dense vegetation, compared to the long pointed wings of plains birds adapted for speed in open air.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Animal survival characteristics in the valley

pages.title: Animal survival characteristics in the valley
pages.body: Valley animals are some of the most impressive in Ghana. The hippopotamus is perfectly adapted to an aquatic life — its eyes, ears and nostrils are positioned on top of its head so it can sense the world while almost completely submerged. Its nearly hairless, thick skin secretes a natural red-tinted fluid that acts as both a sunscreen and an antibiotic, protecting it from sunburn and infection.

Crocodiles are the ultimate ambush predators of the riverbank. Their streamlined bodies and powerful tails make them fast swimmers. They can hold their breath for extended periods, lying submerged and motionless while waiting for prey to approach the water's edge. Their eyes and nostrils, like those of the hippo, are elevated on the head so they can monitor their surroundings while almost invisible in the water. Fish eagles have sharp, curved talons adapted for snatching fish from the water surface, and waterproof feathers that prevent them becoming waterlogged during diving attempts.

> **Lesson 2 Assessment**

questions.q: A structural adaptation is best defined as:
o: A behaviour that helps an organism survive, such as migrating seasonally
A physical feature of an organism's body that improves its survival, such as thick bark or waterproof skin
A change in the environment that forces organisms to adapt quickly
A skill learned from other members of the same species

questions.q: The baobab tree stores water in its enormous trunk. This is an adaptation to:
o: The cool, wet conditions of Ghana's hill forests
The flat, fertile soil of river valleys
The long dry season of the savanna plain
The strong winds of the plateau

questions.q: Which of the following is a correct description of buttress roots?
o: Roots that store water to help trees survive drought
Large flange-like extensions at the base of a tall forest tree that anchor it in shallow soil
Roots that float on the water surface in river valleys
Thin roots that spread widely to absorb dew on the plateau surface

questions.q: The hippopotamus's eyes, ears and nostrils are positioned on top of its head. This adaptation allows it to:
o: See in all directions while running on land
Sense the world while almost completely submerged in water
Hear prey from greater distances than other animals
Detect heat from the sun while resting on the river bank

questions.q: How do epiphyte plants in mountain forests obtain water without roots in soil?
o: They drill roots through tree bark to steal water from the host tree
They store rainwater in hollow stems that can hold water for months
They absorb moisture from the humid air using specialised roots
They obtain all their water from dew that forms on their leaf surfaces at night

questions.q: Which of the following correctly explains why savanna grasses survive the dry season even when all visible parts die back?
o: Their seeds blow away and germinate elsewhere when conditions improve
Their root systems survive underground and produce new growth when the rains return
They store food energy in their seeds which fall to the ground before the dry season
They close their leaf pores completely and enter a state of full dormancy above ground

questions.q: Why do chameleons have independently moving eyes?
o: To change the colour of their eyes to match their surroundings
To look in two different directions at once, providing nearly all-round vision without moving their head
To see ultraviolet light that helps them find food
To detect movement in complete darkness at night

questions.q: The small leaflets of the acacia tree are an adaptation to:
o: Capturing maximum sunlight in the shaded savanna understory
Reducing water loss through evaporation in the dry savanna climate
Storing extra photosynthesis products in case food becomes scarce
Deterring leaf-eating insects by being difficult to chew

questions.q: Hollow, air-filled stems in river plants such as reeds serve what purpose?
o: They make the plant lighter so it floats away from floods
They carry oxygen down to roots growing in waterlogged, oxygen-poor mud
They store water for use during the dry season when river levels drop
They deter grazing animals by making the stems difficult to bite

questions.q: What makes the water hyacinth particularly suited to living in river valleys?
o: It has deep tap roots that anchor it firmly to the river bed
Its air-filled leaf stalks keep it buoyant on the water surface
It has waxy leaves that repel water and allow it to dry quickly after flooding
It can survive without sunlight on the shaded river floor

questions.q: Why do many savanna animals travel long distances during the dry season?
o: To escape bush fires that regularly sweep through the savanna
To find water and pasture, which become scarce as water sources dry up
To breed with animals from other parts of the savanna
To avoid the extreme cold of the dry season nights

questions.q: A monkey's prehensile tail is best described as:
o: A tail used for balance only, similar to that of a cat
A tail that can grasp branches, acting as a fifth limb for movement through the canopy
A tail that changes colour to signal to other monkeys
A tail used to store energy in the same way a camel stores fat in its hump

questions.q: Define adaptation and explain the difference between a structural adaptation and a behavioural adaptation. Give one example of each from organisms in Ghana.
Describe three structural adaptations of the baobab tree that help it survive on the savanna plain.
Explain how the roots of riverside trees in valleys are adapted differently from tree roots on a plateau.
Describe three features of the hippopotamus that make it well suited to valley life.
Explain how epiphytes survive without roots in soil.
Describe the key adaptations of the crocodile that make it an effective ambush predator in a river valley.
Explain how savanna grasses survive the long dry season in northern Ghana.
Describe two adaptations of chameleons that help them survive in mountain forests.
Explain why tall forest trees in Ghana's hill ranges have buttress roots.
Compare the wing shape of a savanna bird (such as a kestrel) with a forest bird. Explain why each shape is suited to its environment.
Describe two ways in which the natural skin of the hippopotamus protects it from environmental hazards.

A scientist discovers a new animal on the Kwahu Plateau. It has large, broad wings, extremely sharp eyesight, and brown-and-gold feathers that match the colour of dry grass. Based on what you have learned about adaptations to plateau environments, describe what this animal probably eats, how it hunts, and what features you would expect in its feet and beak.

Climate change is causing Ghana's northern plains to become hotter and drier. Predict two ways in which animals currently living on the plain might be affected, and suggest one adaptation that could help an animal survive if conditions become significantly more extreme.

Adaptation investigation: Choose one organism from any landform in Ghana (plant or animal). Research its specific adaptations to its habitat. Present your findings as a labelled diagram or annotated drawing, with each labelled feature connected to an explanation of how it helps the organism survive. Present to the class.

Survival challenge: In groups, your teacher will give you a scenario card describing a dramatic change in a landform (for example: the Kwahu Plateau dries out completely; the Volta River stops flooding its valley). Discuss what would happen to the plants and animals in that landform. Which would survive, which would leave, and which might go extinct? Present your predictions with reasons.

My landform album: Create your own personal album of at least eight organisms (four plants and four animals) from the four Ghanaian landforms. For each organism, write or draw: the organism's name, which landform it lives in, and one structural adaptation that helps it survive there. Collect images from magazines, the internet or draw them yourself.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Associations Between Organisms: Mutualism, Parasitism and Commensalism

pages.body:
Look carefully at a flowering plant and you will see bees visiting it. The bee gets nectar; the flower gets its pollen carried to another flower. Both benefit. Now look at a cow with ticks crawling on its skin. The ticks get a blood meal; the cow itches, loses blood and may get disease. One benefits at the other's expense. Now notice a cattle egret following behind a farmer ploughing his field. The bird catches the insects disturbed by the plough; the farmer is neither helped nor harmed. One benefits; the other is unaffected.

- Have you ever noticed any of these kinds of relationships in nature around you?
- Can you think of other examples where two organisms interact in one of these ways?

> **DEFINITION** **Association:** a relationship between two organisms of different species living together or interacting regularly. **Mutualism:** an association between two organisms in which both benefit from the relationship. **Parasitism:** an association in which one organism (the parasite) benefits while the other (the host) is harmed. **Commensalism:** an association in which one organism benefits and the other is neither helped nor harmed.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Mutualism — both organisms benefit

pages.title: Mutualism — both organisms benefit
pages.body:
Mutualism is one of the most important types of interaction in any ecosystem. Many ecosystems could not function without it. The key feature is that both organisms gain something essential from the relationship.

One of the most visible examples of mutualism in Ghana is the relationship between flowers and their pollinators. Bees, butterflies, birds and even some bats visit flowers to collect nectar. In doing so, they accidentally pick up pollen from the flower's stamens. When they visit the next flower of the same species, they deposit some of that pollen on the stigma, enabling fertilisation. The pollinator gets food; the plant gets its pollen transferred. Without this mutualistic relationship, most flowering plants — including many of Ghana's food crops — could not reproduce.

Another important example in Ghanaian farming communities is the relationship between leguminous plants (such as cowpeas, groundnuts and soybeans) and nitrogen-fixing bacteria. Rhizobium bacteria live in nodules on the roots of these plants. The bacteria convert nitrogen gas from the air into a form the plant can use as a nutrient. In return, the plant provides the bacteria with carbohydrates produced by photosynthesis. Both organisms gain — which is why planting legumes improves the soil for subsequent crops.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Associations Between Organisms: Mutualism, Parasitism and Commensalism (part 3)

pages.body:
In river valleys and near grazing areas, the oxpecker bird often sits on the backs of cattle, buffalo and other large mammals. The oxpecker eats ticks, flies and parasites from the animal's skin. The animal gets relief from irritating parasites and a warning signal when the bird takes flight. Both benefit, though scientists continue to study whether the oxpecker also causes some harm by keeping wounds open.

In termite mounds on the savanna plain, a community of organisms lives alongside the termites — including certain beetles and fungi. Some fungi are cultivated by the termites as a food source, while the fungi break down plant material that the termites cannot digest alone. This cultivated farming relationship benefits both parties.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Parasitism — one benefits, the other is harmed

pages.title: Parasitism — one benefits, the other is harmed
pages.body:
Parasitism is extremely common in nature. A parasite lives in or on a host, taking nutrients or using the host's body in a way that harms it. The parasite benefits; the host suffers. Importantly, most parasites do not immediately kill their hosts, because a dead host provides no further benefit. However, heavy parasite loads weaken and may eventually kill the host.

Ticks are a familiar example in Ghana's farming communities. They attach to the skin of cattle, goats and other animals and feed on their blood. Heavy tick infestations cause anaemia, skin damage and can transmit diseases such as East Coast Fever. The tick benefits; the animal is harmed. Farmers spend considerable time and money applying acaricides (tick-killing chemicals) to their animals.

The Striga plant, also called witchweed, is one of the most damaging agricultural parasites in northern Ghana. Striga attaches its roots to the roots of cereal crops such as maize, sorghum and millet. It withdraws water, nutrients and even carbohydrates from the crop's root system. Striga can reduce maize yields by 40 to 80 percent in heavily infested fields. The Striga plant benefits; the crop is severely harmed.

Internal parasites are also common. Intestinal worms such as roundworms and tapeworms live inside the digestive tracts of humans and animals, absorbing food that the host has digested. In children, heavy worm infections cause malnutrition, anaemia and impaired development. The worm benefits; the child is harmed.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Commensalism — one benefits, the other is unaffected

pages.body: Malaria is caused by a parasitic organism — Plasmodium — carried by the female Anopheles mosquito. The Plasmodium parasite benefits from living and reproducing inside the human body. The human host suffers fever, organ damage and can die. Malaria remains one of Ghana's most serious public health challenges.

pages.title: Commensalism — one benefits, the other is unaffected
pages.body:
Commensalism is the most neutral of the three associations. One organism benefits; the other is genuinely unaffected — neither harmed nor helped. This is also the hardest association to confirm in real life, because biologists continue to discover that what appears neutral often has subtle effects in one direction or the other.

The cattle egret is a good example often cited in Ghana. These white birds follow closely behind cattle, farmers ploughing, or elephants moving through the grass. They catch grasshoppers, frogs and other small animals that are disturbed by the large animal's movement. The cattle egret benefits by gaining food it would struggle to catch otherwise. The cattle or elephant is generally unaffected — it neither benefits from nor is harmed by the bird's presence.

Many of the orchids and mosses growing on tree branches in Ghana's forest hills practice commensalism. These epiphytes use the tree's height and structure to gain access to light, but they do not take nutrients from the tree's vascular system. The epiphyte benefits from the elevated position; the tree is unaffected.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Effects of associations on habitats

pages.body: In the ocean and in rivers, small fish often shelter among sea anemones, coral formations or the bodies of larger fish. The small fish gain protection from predators by staying close to something dangerous or well-defended. The larger organism is typically unaffected by the presence of these small hitchhikers.

pages.title: Effects of associations on habitats
pages.body: These three types of association together shape the way ecosystems function. Mutualism creates networks of interdependence — remove the bees from a forest and the flowering plants cannot reproduce, leading to collapse of the whole food web above them. Parasitism keeps populations in check — parasites often preferentially affect sick or weak individuals, indirectly improving the overall health of the host population. Commensalism allows organisms to exploit available opportunities without causing harm.

When an invasive parasite enters an ecosystem where organisms have no evolved resistance to it, the damage can be catastrophic. The Striga weed — believed to have increased in northern Ghana due to soil degradation — is devastating because local maize varieties were not evolved to resist its particular parasitic strategy. Understanding these associations helps farmers, conservationists and doctors manage ecosystems, farms and public health more effectively.

> **Lesson 3 Assessment**

questions.q: Which of the following correctly defines mutualism?
o: An association in which one organism benefits while the other is unaffected
An association in which both organisms benefit from the relationship
An association in which one organism harms the other while gaining benefit
An association in which both organisms are harmed by living together

questions.q: In the relationship between leguminous plants and Rhizobium bacteria, which statement is correct?
o: The bacteria harm the plant by taking nutrients from its roots
The plant harms the bacteria by crowding them out of the soil
Both the bacteria and the plant benefit: bacteria get carbohydrates; the plant gets usable nitrogen
The plant benefits by getting nitrogen while the bacteria are unaffected

questions.q: Ticks feeding on cattle is an example of which type of association?
o: Mutualism
Commensalism
Parasitism
Predation

questions.q: Why do most parasites NOT immediately kill their hosts?
o: Parasites cannot harm organisms that are larger than themselves
A living host provides ongoing benefits to the parasite; a dead host is useless
Parasites are too small to cause enough harm to kill a large host
Most parasites form a mutualistic relationship with the host over time

questions.q: Which of the following is the best example of commensalism?
o: Bees collecting nectar and pollinating flowers in return
Ticks feeding on cattle blood and causing anaemia
Cattle egrets catching insects disturbed by grazing cattle, without affecting the cattle
Rhizobium bacteria providing nitrogen to leguminous plants in exchange for carbohydrates

questions.q: The Striga plant is a devastating agricultural parasite in northern Ghana because it:
o: Produces toxins that poison the soil and kill nearby plants
Attaches its roots to cereal crop roots and withdraws water, nutrients and carbohydrates
Spreads rapidly by producing thousands of seeds that germinate in the rainy season
Shades out crops by growing taller than them and blocking their sunlight

questions.q: Malaria is caused by a parasitic organism called Plasmodium. Which statement about this parasite is correct?
o: Plasmodium is a virus that is carried by the Aedes mosquito
Plasmodium is a parasitic organism carried by female Anopheles mosquitoes that lives and reproduces inside human red blood cells
Plasmodium is a bacterial parasite transmitted by drinking contaminated water
Plasmodium is a fungal parasite that infects only animals, not humans

questions.q: Epiphytic orchids growing on tree branches in a forest hill are an example of commensalism because:
o: They steal nutrients from the tree's vascular system while giving nothing in return
The tree provides them with nutrients and water through the bark
They use the tree's height and structure to access light without taking anything from the tree
They pollinate the tree's flowers in return for using the tree's surface

questions.q: Which of the following explains why mutualistic associations are important for ecosystem stability?
o: They reduce the number of organisms in an ecosystem, making it more manageable
They create networks of interdependence; removing one partner can cause the collapse of systems that depend on it
They make organisms more competitive, leading to the survival of the strongest
They replace parasitic relationships and prevent harmful associations from developing

questions.q: In the oxpecker-cattle relationship, what benefit does the cattle receive?
o: Nutrients from the food that the oxpecker shares
Removal of ticks and parasites from its skin, and warning signals when the bird takes flight
Protection from predators who fear the oxpecker
Grooming of its fur that improves insulation in cold weather

questions.q: Why is the Striga plant particularly damaging in northern Ghana's farms?
o: It directly attacks the farmer rather than the crops
It was introduced from Europe where maize varieties had evolved resistance to it; Ghanaian varieties had not
Local maize varieties have no evolved resistance to Striga's parasitic strategy, and soil degradation has increased its spread
It only grows during the dry season when farmers cannot remove it

questions.q: Which of the following associations would have the most severe consequences if the beneficial partner were removed from an ecosystem?
o: Commensalism between a cattle egret and cattle
Mutualism between bees and flowering plants, because removing bees disrupts pollination of most food crops
Parasitism between ticks and cattle, because the ticks control cattle populations
Commensalism between epiphytic orchids and forest trees

questions.q: Define mutualism, parasitism and commensalism. Give one Ghanaian example of each.
Explain the mutualistic relationship between leguminous plants and Rhizobium bacteria. Why is this relationship important for Ghanaian farmers?
Describe the relationship between bees and flowering plants. Which type of association is this and why?
Explain how the Striga plant is a parasite of cereal crops. Describe the harm it causes to maize plants in Ghana.
Describe the cattle egret-cattle relationship and explain why it is classified as commensalism rather than mutualism.
What is Plasmodium and how does it harm its human host? What organism carries it?
Explain why mutualistic associations are critical to the functioning of ecosystems. Use the example of pollinators and flowering plants.
Explain why parasites do not usually kill their hosts immediately. What would happen to the parasite if the host died?
Describe the relationship between epiphytic orchids and forest trees. Is this mutualism, parasitism or commensalism? Explain your classification.
Explain how parasitism can sometimes have an indirect positive effect on a population, even though it harms individual hosts.
Describe how the introduction of an invasive parasite into an ecosystem where organisms have no evolved resistance can be devastating. Use a specific Ghanaian example.

A farmer in the Upper East Region notices that her cowpeas (a leguminous plant) are growing much better than her maize on the same farm. After the cowpea harvest, the soil where they grew produces healthier maize the following season. Using your knowledge of associations, explain what happened in the soil under the cowpeas, and recommend how she could use this knowledge to improve all her crops.

A school science club is studying a forest near their community. They observe: (a) moss growing on the bark of trees, (b) ticks on a deer, and (c) bees visiting wildflowers. Classify each observation as mutualism, parasitism or commensalism, and explain your reasoning for each classification.

Association hunt: Over one week, observe the area around your school and home for examples of organisms interacting. Record at least five interactions. For each one, identify the two organisms involved, describe what each organism gains or loses, and classify the interaction as mutualism, parasitism or commensalism. Present your findings to the class.

Research and presentation: Research one of the following associations in depth and present your findings to the class: (a) the mutualistic relationship between mycorrhizal fungi and tree roots, (b) the parasitic relationship between the Plasmodium parasite and humans (malaria), (c) the mutualistic relationship between fig trees and fig wasps. Include: which organisms are involved, what each organism gains, where this association is found in Ghana, and its importance for the ecosystem.

Ecosystem impact analysis: Choose one of the three types of association (mutualism, parasitism or commensalism) and, in groups, investigate what would happen to a specific Ghanaian ecosystem if all examples of that association were suddenly removed. For example: what would happen to the savanna if all parasitic relationships were eliminated? Write a group report and present it to the class.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Word bank

pages.body:
| **Word** | **What it means** |
|---|---|
| Landform | A natural physical feature of the Earth's surface such as a mountain, plain, valley or plateau |
| Habitat | The specific environment in which an organism lives |
| Adaptation | A feature of an organism's body or behaviour that helps it survive in its habitat |
| Structural adaptation | A physical body feature that aids survival |
| Behavioural adaptation | An action or behaviour pattern that aids survival |
| Plateau | A high, flat area of land raised above surrounding countryside (e.g. Kwahu Plateau) |
| Plain | A large flat or gently rolling area of land at low altitude (e.g. northern savanna) |
| Gallery forest | Dense tree growth along the banks of a river in an otherwise open landscape |
| Epiphyte | A plant that grows on another plant for physical support without taking nutrients from it |
| Buttress root | A large, flange-like root extension at the base of a tall forest tree providing stability |
| Association | A relationship between two different species living together or interacting regularly |
| Mutualism | An association in which both organisms benefit |
| Parasitism | An association in which one organism (the parasite) benefits and the other (the host) is harmed |
| Commensalism | An association in which one organism benefits and the other is unaffected |
| Host | An organism in or on which a parasite lives |
| Parasite | An organism that lives in or on a host and benefits at the host's expense |
| Striga | A parasitic flowering plant that attaches to cereal crop roots, reducing yields |
| Rhizobium | Nitrogen-fixing bacteria that live in root nodules of leguminous plants in a mutualistic relationship |
| Pollinator | An animal (bee, butterfly, bird) that carries pollen between flowers, enabling plant reproduction |
